```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

Top business journals disagree about how a regression table should look. The *American Economic Review* and the *Strategic Management Journal* do not allow significance stars; *Contemporary Accounting Research* wants them in the same cell as the estimate with t-statistics underneath; the *Journal of Marketing* wants exact three-digit p-values and no leading zeros; the *Journal of Finance* numbers tables I, II, III. Figures differ too: column widths, minimum resolution, fonts, whether the title may sit inside the image, whether the print edition is grayscale, and whether alt text is required.

causalverse stores these rules for the 54 journals on the FT50 (2016 and April 2026 lists) and the UTD24, and applies them when it exports.

```{r}
library(causalverse)
library(ggplot2)
```

## The journals covered

```{r}
jl <- journal_list()
nrow(jl)
c(ft50 = sum(jl$ft50_2026), ft50_2016 = sum(jl$ft50_2016), utd24 = sum(jl$utd24))
table(jl$confidence)
```

`confidence` says how each style was sourced: `"high"` means the journal's own current guidelines were read in full; `"medium"` means an older copy, search-engine text or partly publisher-wide rules; `"low"` means only the publisher's general rules could be read. Check the low-confidence ones by hand before a submission.

## Look up one journal

```{r}
journal_style("smj")
```

## How the rules differ

```{r}
rule_row <- function(id) {
  s <- journal_style(id)
  t <- s$table; f <- s$figure
  data.frame(
    journal      = s$abbrev,
    stars        = switch(t$significance, stars = paste(names(t$stars), t$stars, sep = "", collapse = " "),
                          none = "banned", exact_p = "exact p"),
    parentheses  = t$uncertainty,
    leading_zero = t$leading_zero,
    numbering    = t$numbering,
    tables_go    = t$placement,
    line_art_dpi = f$dpi[["line_art"]],
    width_mm     = paste(f$widths_mm[["single"]], f$widths_mm[["double"]], sep = "/"),
    grayscale    = f$grayscale,
    alt_text     = f$alt_text
  )
}
ids <- c("aer", "jf", "qje", "rfs", "jfqa", "tar", "car", "jm", "jcr", "mnsc",
         "misq", "amj", "asq", "smj", "jibs", "jap", "jbv", "jbe")
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(ids, rule_row)), row.names = FALSE)
```

## One set of models, many journals

```{r}
models <- list(
  "(1)" = lm(mpg ~ am, data = mtcars),
  "(2)" = lm(mpg ~ am + wt, data = mtcars),
  "(3)" = lm(mpg ~ am + wt + hp, data = mtcars)
)
labels <- c(am = "Manual transmission", wt = "Weight", hp = "Horsepower")
```

**American Economic Review**: no stars, standard errors in parentheses, leading zeros.

```{r}
journal_table(models, "aer", title = "Transmission and Fuel Economy", coef_map = labels)
```

**Journal of Finance**: stars at 10/5/1%, Roman table numbers.

```{r}
journal_table(models, "jf", title = "Transmission and Fuel Economy", number = 2, coef_map = labels)
```

**Strategic Management Journal**: no stars, "TABLE 1 Name" caption, tables after the references.

```{r}
journal_table(models, "smj", title = "Transmission and fuel economy", coef_map = labels)
```

**Journal of Marketing**: no stars, exact p-values, no leading zeros, a title that states the takeaway.

```{r}
journal_table(models, "jm", title = "Manual Cars Are Not More Efficient Once Weight Is Held Constant",
              coef_map = labels)
```

**Academy of Management Journal**: two decimals and the AOM dagger/star stack.

```{r}
journal_table(models, "amj", title = "Transmission and Fuel Economy", coef_map = labels)
```

**Contemporary Accounting Research**: t-statistics in parentheses, upper-case label, sentence-case title ending in a period.

```{r}
journal_table(models, "car", title = "Transmission and fuel economy", coef_map = labels,
              source = "mtcars data (Henderson and Velleman 1981)")
```

**Journal of Consumer Research**: 95% confidence intervals and exact p-values, centred upper-case caption.

```{r}
journal_table(models, "jcr", title = "Transmission and fuel economy", coef_map = labels)
```

**Management Science** (all INFORMS journals): bold run-in "Table 1." label, the note order Source, Note, footnotes, p-values.

```{r}
journal_table(models, "mnsc", title = "Transmission and Fuel Economy", coef_map = labels,
              notes = "OLS estimates.", source = "mtcars data.")
```

### Exporting

`export_tab()` writes the same table to LaTeX (booktabs + threeparttable), Word, HTML and Excel. Word matters for AOM and SAGE journals, which ask for editable Word tables. For journals that want tables at the end of the manuscript, it also tells you which callout to put in the text.

```{r}
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "submission")
files <- export_tab(models, "table1", out, journal = "smj",
                    title = "Transmission and fuel economy", coef_map = labels,
                    formats = c("tex", "html", "xlsx"))
basename(files)
```

The HTML version, as it would appear in a manuscript:

```{r, results = "asis"}
cat(readLines(file.path(out, "table1.html")), sep = "\n")
```

### Checking a table against another journal

A table built for one journal can be checked against another before you resubmit elsewhere:

```{r}
jf_table <- journal_table(models, "jf", coef_map = labels)
journal_check(jf_table, "aer")
```

## Figures

The same scatter plot, checked against the *Journal of Marketing*, which prints in grayscale and wants the title in the caption:

```{r, fig.width = 3.5, fig.height = 2.8}
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = factor(cyl), shape = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  labs(title = "Heavier cars travel fewer miles per gallon",
       x = "Weight (1,000 lbs)", y = "Miles per gallon",
       colour = "Cylinders", shape = "Cylinders")
journal_check(p, "jm")
```

`theme_journal()` and `scale_colour_journal()` fix both problems: gray levels 20% apart (AMA's rule), Arial, sizes in points at the printed width, and no title in the image.

```{r, fig.width = 3.5, fig.height = 2.8}
p_jm <- p + scale_colour_journal("jm") + theme_journal("jm")
journal_check(p_jm, "jm")
p_jm
```

For a journal that prints in colour, the scale uses viridis, whose lightness rises steadily so the groups still separate in grayscale:

```{r, fig.width = 3.5, fig.height = 2.8}
p + scale_colour_journal("mnsc") + theme_journal("mnsc")
```

`export_fig()` saves at the journal's column width and resolution, in its preferred formats, and writes the caption (with the title moved out of the image), notes and alt text to a text file:

```{r}
res <- export_fig(p_jm, "figure1", out, journal = "rfs", stage = "final",
                  alt_text = "Scatter plot in which miles per gallon fall as weight rises.")
basename(res$files)
c(width_mm = res$width_mm, dpi = res$dpi)
res$caption
```

The same call for other journals picks up their rules, for example Elsevier's 1000 dpi for line art and 90 mm columns:

```{r}
sapply(c("jfe", "jbe", "smj", "aer", "mnsc"), function(j) {
  f <- journal_style(j)$figure
  c(single_mm = f$widths_mm[["single"]], line_art_dpi = f$dpi[["line_art"]],
    formats = paste(f$formats_final, collapse = "+"))
})
```

## Keeping the rules current

Every rule comes from the URLs listed by `journal_sources()`:

```{r}
journal_sources("jm")
```

A GitHub Action (`.github/workflows/journal-guidelines.yaml`) fetches every one of these pages each week, reduces each page to its text, and compares it with the last snapshot. When a page changes, it opens a pull request showing the changed lines. A maintainer then updates the journal's entry in `R/journal_styles_data.R`. Pages whose sites block automated visitors are checked through the Internet Archive; pages that cannot be reached either way are listed in the pull request for manual review.

Each style also records the date its rules were verified. `journal_style()` warns when that date is more than six months old, so a stale rule set does not go unnoticed.
